observed.reply:
In **Chapter 9** of *The Adventures of Pinocchio*, Pinocchio tells himself:

“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,”

The useful part of that passage isn’t that it proves anything about your character. It shows a present choice being made more comfortable by a sincere-sounding promise about the future. Your hope of making things up to your sister can be genuine, while still not changing what happens during the study evening she has made possible for you.

So perhaps the gap to examine is not “Do I care?” but “What does the promise of making it up later allow me to postpone tonight?” That keeps responsibility in view without turning one recurring pattern into “I’m a terrible person.” What tends to happen in the few minutes when one of those study evenings is about to begin?

evidence.text:
See Pinocchio hurrying off to school with his new A-B-C book under
his arm! As he walked along, his brain was busy planning hundreds of
wonderful things, building hundreds of castles in the air. Talking to
himself, he said:

“In school today, I’ll learn to read, tomorrow to write, and the day
after tomorrow I’ll do arithmetic. Then, clever as I am, I can earn a
lot of money. With the very first pennies I make, I’ll buy Father a new
cloth coat. Cloth, did I say? No, it shall be of gold and silver with
diamond buttons. That poor man certainly deserves it; for, after all,
isn’t he in his shirt sleeves because he was good enough to buy a
book for me? On this cold day, too! Fathers are indeed good to their
children!”

As he talked to himself, he thought he heard sounds of pipes and drums
coming from a distance: pi-pi-pi, pi-pi-pi. . .zum, zum, zum, zum.

He stopped to listen. Those sounds came from a little street that led to
a small village along the shore.

“What can that noise be? What a nuisance that I have to go to school!
Otherwise. . .”

There he stopped, very much puzzled. He felt he had to make up his mind
for either one thing or another. Should he go to school, or should he
follow the pipes?

“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,” decided the little rascal at
last, shrugging his shoulders.

No sooner said than done. He started down the street, going like the
wind. On he ran, and louder grew the sounds of pipe and drum: pi-pi-pi,
pi-pi-pi, pi-pi-pi . . .zum, zum, zum, zum.

Suddenly, he found himself in a large square, full of people standing in
front of a little wooden building painted in brilliant colors.

“What is that house?” Pinocchio asked a little boy near him.

“Read the sign and you’ll know.”

“I’d like to read, but somehow I can’t today.”

observed.input_line: My sister is covering my chores for a course I'm taking; I picture making it up to her when I qualify, but I keep wasting the study evenings she gives me. Can you help me work out one small way to honour her help this week, without turning a missed evening into 'I'm a terrible person'?

context_resolution.explanation: No confirmed book or reading boundary yet; Muse will call librarian_route during its own turn if the request appears to depend on a specific book.

observed.reply:
Try making this week’s way of honouring her help **small, visible, and separate from your performance**: send her a message thanking her specifically for covering your chores, then choose one modest act you can reliably do—perhaps taking back one chore for a day, making her tea, or leaving a note—without making it conditional on qualifying.

For the study evenings, set a deliberately low bar: **one 20-minute session** with a clear first task. If an evening goes by, call it a missed evening, not a verdict on you. You can say: “I didn’t use that evening well, but I’m still grateful for what you made possible, and I’m going to try again tomorrow.”

The aim this week isn’t to prove you deserve her help. It’s to acknowledge it and make one honest next use of it.

“It was too warm.”

his tears, he jumped on his father’s neck and kissed him over and over.
